props.title: Our Daily Bread

sections.content: Our Daily Bread revolutionized food documentary filmmaking through its stark, dialogue-free observation of industrial food production. Director Nikolaus Geyrhalter's clinical approach differs sharply from activist docs like Food, Inc. (2008) or Super Size Me (2004). Instead of narration or interviews, he lets the mechanized choreography of modern food production speak for itself. The film's pristine compositions and lengthy static shots transform agricultural facilities into something approaching science fiction, reminiscent of the sterile environments in THX 1138 (1971) or Silent Running (1972).

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later observational documentaries about food systems and industrial processes. Leviathan (2012) applies a similar immersive approach to commercial fishing, while Workingman's Death (2005) examines dangerous manual labor through the same detached lens. The mechanical precision captured in Our Daily Bread inspired sequences in fiction films like Samsara (2011) and Manufactured Landscapes (2006), which similarly transform industrial spaces into hypnotic visual compositions.

What sets Our Daily Bread apart is its refusal to moralize. Unlike Fast Food Nation (2006) or Fed Up (2014), Geyrhalter doesn't explicitly critique industrial agriculture. The film's power comes from simply showing the scale and automation of modern food production, letting viewers draw their own conclusions. This approach influenced later documentaries like The Signal Hill Anthology (2012) and In the Course of Time (2007), which similarly trust in the power of pure observation. sections.content: The film marked a significant shift away from the Michael Moore-style activist documentary that dominated the early 2000s. Rather than following Food, Inc.'s (2008) approach of expert interviews and dramatic revelations, Our Daily Bread proves that careful observation can be more powerful than overt argumentation. This influenced later films like Sweetgrass (2009) and Sleep Furiously (2008), which similarly eschew traditional documentary techniques in favor of patient observation.
